newsitem.title: USA: Chicago Fed focuses on technology and bank risk.
newsitem.headline: Chicago Fed focuses on technology and bank risk.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Michael Moskow said on Thursday technology changes may result in new risk and solutions for the banking sector.
"Technology is blurring the old lines that define products and services, customers and markets," Moskow told the Chicago Fed's Conference on Bank Structure and Competition.

"No matter how effective our tools, a bank's risk profile can change," Moskow said, stressing that banks must "have systems in place that continually monitor and manage risk to take advantage of the sophisticated technology that has improved risk management."
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, in his keynote address to the conference attended by bankers, experts and regulators, focused on risk management as well.
"The folly of attempting to legislate or regulate against the primal forces of the market is one of the most fundamental lessons learned by banking reegulators," Greenspan said.
The Fed chairman stressed that bankers' and regulators' ability to address technology changes will ensure "the benefits of financial stability that are critical to our economy."
The Chicago Fed president pointed out the importance for banks to have in place effective risk management mechanisms.

"It's these systems and the accountability of bank management for their effective operation that is a key to effective supervision," Moskow said. "How bankers and supervisors respond to these issues will help shape the future of the industry."
The Chicago Fed conference will cover how three main areas respond to technology changes -- financial services, financial markets and regulatory authorities.
Outlining the conference's goals, Moskow earlier said the focus will be on evaluating "the opportunities and concerns raised by technological innovations."

Moskow noted such developments bring "into question the appropriateness of regulations concerning service offerings, geographic and ownership restrictions, traditional anti-trust enforcement and the very framework of the existing regulatory structure."
"We intend to emphasize risk management and bank capital regulation and bank anti-trust regulation," Moskow also said.
The Chicago Fed began holding annual conferences on banking in 1963 to discuss the different challenges faced by the U.S. banking industry.

It advocated industry deregulation in the 1970s and focused on risk management issues in the 1980s as the U.S. banking industry faced mounting assets quality problems. The conference also dealt with consumer issues, such as community reinvestment and discrimination in lending.

The Chicago Fed also studied the role of the Fed in the payments system and the scope and pricing of financial services the Fed System provides to the banking industry. That issue is central to the future of the Fed System and is the object of a special commission led by Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin.
Other Fed officials to address the conference are Boston Fed President Cathy Minehan and Fed Governor Susan Phillips.
